archetype.name: Gunslinger (sack-prone)
archetype.definition: A nine-year starter who has always pushed the ball and lived with the interceptions and long-held sacks that come with it. This year the downside of that style is outweighing the payoff in a run-first offense.

report.headline: The sacks and close-game stalls, not the arm, are sinking Mayfield's season
report.take:
Mayfield has been the same quarterback for most of his career: aggressive, willing to hold the ball, near the bottom of the league in interceptions almost every year, and good enough to carry an offense when the ball comes out on time. His 2024 peak came when he was at his quickest and cleanest: 2.7 seconds to throw, aggressiveness down to 10.9%, a bad-throw rate fifth-best in the league and 0.207 EPA per play. 2025 slid back toward his norm at 0.089. In 2026 he has fallen through the floor: -0.217 EPA per dropback, 46th of 54, with a 2-4 record in his starts.

The cause is narrow and identifiable. He is pressured on only 25% of dropbacks, 31st of 42, so this is not a line getting beaten every snap. But 45% of those pressures end in sacks, the worst rate among 42 qualifiers, and his time to throw has crept up to 2.96 seconds. That produces an 11.3% sack rate against a league average of 7.9. Those sacks land in the worst spots. Within one score he is at -0.476 EPA per play, with 15 of his 18 sacks. On third down the Bucs convert 27.5% while facing 8.6 yards to go on average. The offense sets him up badly too: Todd Bowles runs a run-first team with the league's second-best defense and a pass rate 7.5 points under expectation, 30th. So many of his dropbacks are obvious passing downs out of shotgun. There he posts -0.271 EPA per play, against -0.064 and a 46.9% success rate under center.

The arm is not the main problem. Throws of 10-plus air yards have added positive EPA overall while everything under 10 has bled it away. He is at +0.134 per play in the intermediate range and +0.358 over the middle. The underneath game is where things break: three of his four interceptions came on throws of 0-9 yards, and his screens behind the line lose value despite an 86.2% completion rate. That screen volume flatters his CPOE, which ranks 26th, and so does a mid-26th standing that sits above league average. The tracking CPOE is negative, and his bad-throw rate of 18.3% is up 3.2 points from last year. His 2.1% TD rate against a league 4.0% looks like red-zone noise on 30 plays, not a lost skill. The three lost fumbles all came in Week 1. His best splits come with the Bucs trailing by 9 or more, and soft coverage helps those.

The outlook depends on health and volume more than talent. He returned in Weeks 7-8 to throw only 11 and 3 passes in two wins, then threw 32 times in a loss at Chicago and hurt his foot and ankle. He enters the bye listed questionable. A run-first team that already started Jalon Daniels for three weeks has no reason to lean on a hobbled quarterback with a sack problem unless the scoreboard forces it. Expect TD rate to climb toward normal. Do not expect the sack rate to fix itself, because it has been part of his game for years.

strengths.title: Intermediate and middle-of-field throws
strengths.body: When he gets the ball 10-plus yards downfield, especially between the numbers, he still produces positive plays. That fits his career aDOT profile. It also lines up with Chris Godwin Jr., his most efficient target, and it is the version of his game that won in 2023-24. The samples are small, 35 intermediate and 22 middle throws, but it is a trait he has shown for years, not a fluke.

strengths.title: Efficient from under center
strengths.body: Under center, where play-action and the run threat keep the rush honest, he completes 72.4% with a 10.7 CPOE and a 46.9% success rate. That is close to a functional starter's line. The gap against his shotgun numbers says the issue is the situations he is put in, not his reads on early downs. It should hold as long as the Bucs keep leaning on the run game, which ranks 9th by EPA.

strengths.title: Scrambles still pay
strengths.body: His 10 scrambles have averaged 0.225 EPA and produced four first downs, so extending plays still creates something. That is the upside of his habit of holding the ball. A foot and ankle sprain is the biggest threat to it, since his rushing has already dropped from 22.5 yards a game last year.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He converts pressure into sacks at the worst rate among qualifiers even though he is not pressured unusually often. His time to throw is up to 2.96 seconds. This is a heightened version of who he has always been: his pressure-to-sack rate was 39.1% last year and above 35% in most seasons. The extended plays and scrambles do not come close to paying for 51 sacks on a 17-game pace. Expect some improvement but not a cure.

concerns.title: Collapse in close games and on third down
concerns.body: Within one score he has been one of the least efficient passers anywhere: -0.476 EPA per play, with 15 sacks. Third down has gone the same way. Long yardage, shotgun and a defense that knows the pass is coming combine with his sack habit, and the no-huddle snaps have been even worse. Some of this is the run-first offense leaving him behind the chains. Even so, it is the core of his negative EPA, and it is what keeps the Bucs from trusting him.

concerns.title: Turnovers and a throttled role
concerns.body: Three interceptions on short throws and six turnover-worthy fumbles show loose ball security, even if the three lost fumbles all came in one game. Combined with the foot injury and a team passing well under expectation, his volume has shrunk to 15.3 attempts a game over his last three. That caps what he can produce even when he plays well.

trend.note: Week 1 brought a 14 CPOE but three lost fumbles. Weeks 2-3 sank to double-digit negative EPA, with six sacks against Minnesota's now-top defense. After three weeks out he threw 11 and 3 passes in two wins, then posted 243 yards with two picks at Chicago. His last-three EPA per dropback of -0.206 is essentially his season mark, so the volume has swung while the efficiency has not moved.

nextGame.headline: Depleted Lions secondary invites volume, if the foot cooperates
nextGame.body:
On paper, Detroit is the most inviting pass defense he has seen. The Lions rank 24th in pass EPA and allow 20.8 PPR points a game to quarterbacks, 31st. Offenses pass on them 5.4 points more than normal, the second-strongest pass funnel in the league. Detroit's offense ranks 5th in pass EPA, and the Lions are 6.5-point favorites at home with a 46.5 total, so the Bucs may have to throw rather than grind. Trailing is where his numbers have looked best, though soft coverage props that up. The risk is the same one as all season: Detroit's 8.2% sack rate ranks 4th, against a quarterback who turns pressure into sacks more than anyone. The game is indoors, so weather is not a factor.

Availability tilts toward him on the other side. Aidan Hutchinson is out with a torn ACL, which takes away the Lions' main edge rusher, and that matters more for this quarterback than almost any other. CB D.J. Reed, a 94% snap starter, is out, safety Kerby Joseph is out, and LB Jack Campbell, a 97% snap player, is on IR. That leaves holes at every level of the coverage. Mayfield himself is questionable with a foot and ankle sprain from Week 9 and has had a bye to heal. If he plays limited, the run-first Bucs will shrink his role further, and his already minimal rushing is likely to vanish.

keyMatchups.title: Sack-prone QB vs Lions pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gets home often, ranking 5th in hit rate and 4th in sack rate, and his 45% pressure-to-sack rate is the league's worst. Without Hutchinson the rush should be less dangerous, but it remains the most likely way this game goes wrong for him.

keyMatchups.title: Pass funnel with secondary holes
keyMatchups.body: Offenses throw more against Detroit than against almost anyone, and the Lions give up big pass plays, ranking 26th in explosive pass rate. With Reed and Joseph out, his intermediate and middle-of-field throws, the part of his game that still works, have room.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end hole for Otton
keyMatchups.body: Detroit is among the worst defenses against lead tight ends, by both points over average and EPA per target. Cade Otton leads the team in targets but has been a drain at -0.218 EPA per target. This is the spot where that could flip.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Bucs let him throw from shotgun on early downs or hide him under center, and how fast he gets the ball out against a Lions rush without Hutchinson.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts most likely to improve are touchdowns and turnovers luck. A 2.1% TD rate from a quarterback who threw 26 and 41 touchdowns the last two years is mostly red-zone noise on a small sample, and three lost fumbles in one game will not repeat at that rate. If he is healthy, 0.8 to 1.3 passing TDs a game is a reasonable range. The parts likely to stick are the sacks and the volume. Holding the ball has been his trait for years, and the Bucs' identity of an elite defense, a decent run game and pass rates well under expectation limits his attempts unless they fall behind. That points to roughly 160 to 220 passing yards a game, more in shootouts and less in the low-scoring wins this defense produces.

Some efficiency recovery is likely, because his downfield work and under-center play are better than his overall line suggests. But a return to his 2024 level would need the ball to come out faster, and nothing in his last three games shows that yet. The foot injury is the biggest unknown: it threatens his scrambling, his platform in the pocket and his hold on the job, with Jalon Daniels already having started three games this year.
swingFactors: Foot/ankle health and whether Jalon Daniels gets more starts
Whether time to throw and pressure-to-sack come down
How often game script forces the run-first Bucs to pass

confidence.note: Only 142 attempts, two near-zero-volume games, a current foot injury, and a mid-season QB switch distort the sample.
